<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    Road-salt use has increased steadily across cold regions, raising concerns about the long-term accumulation of chloride (Cl
                    <jats:sup>−</jats:sup>
                    ) and sodium (Na
                    <jats:sup>+</jats:sup>
                    ) in streams and groundwater. Karst watersheds may be particularly sensitive to these inputs because rapid recharge and extensive subsurface flowpaths can transport and store dissolved ions. We analyzed two decades (1999–2020) of Cl
                    <jats:sup>−</jats:sup>
                    and Na
                    <jats:sup>+</jats:sup>
                    data from 15 streams and 8 springs in the Spring Creek watershed of central Pennsylvania to evaluate spatial patterns, long-term and seasonal trends, and watershed characteristics associated with solute behavior. Concentrations varied widely across the basin and increased systematically with watershed development. Using the Weighted Regressions on Time, Discharge, and Season modeling approach, we found significant upward flow-normalized (FN) Cl
                    <jats:sup>−</jats:sup>
                    trends at all gaged stream sites (
                    <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                    < 0.05), with widespread but generally smaller increases in Na
                    <jats:sup>+</jats:sup>
                    , based on baseflow-oriented sampling. Springs showed the steepest long-term increases, consistent with solute storage and gradual release from groundwater. Cl
                    <jats:sup>−</jats:sup>
                    concentrations were typically highest during summer baseflow, and long-term increases were positively related to baseflow index, underscoring the role of groundwater pathways. To evaluate multiple watershed controls simultaneously, we developed random forest models, which explained most of the spatial variability in annual FN concentrations and identified developed land cover as the strongest predictor, followed by carbonate bedrock, drainage area, and proximity to roads. Our results show that both land use and groundwater pathways strongly shape the persistence of road-salt ions in this mixed land use karst watershed. Groundwater storage plays a central role in sustaining elevated Cl
                    <jats:sup>−</jats:sup>
                    and Na
                    <jats:sup>+</jats:sup>
                    in this karstic system, indicating that stream concentrations may respond slowly to any future changes in road-salt application.
                  </jats:p>
title: Road salt impacts on streams and springs in a karstic watershed
